findings.issue_text: Providers with the same highest `order()` are silently selected by ServiceLoader iteration order, so default and FIPS providers can nondeterministically select the non-FIPS provider instead of failing fast.

Adding `order()` as an abstract method breaks external `CryptoProvider` SPI implementations: source consumers no longer compile and already-built providers can throw `AbstractMethodError` during `CryptoIntegration.init`.
`concatenatedRSToASN1DER` does not validate `signature.length == signLength`, so trailing bytes are truncated and malformed non-canonical JWS ECDSA signatures may be accepted.
ECDSA tests use platform-default EC keys for ES384 and ES512, so they do not test the required 48- and 66-byte coordinate curves or verify those algorithms work with their required curves.

goldens.comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

adjudication_records.issue_text: `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` does not validate `signature.length == signLength`, so trailing bytes are truncated and malformed non-canonical JWS ECDSA signatures may be accepted.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` method in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java, the code copies `len` bytes (signLength/2) from the signature array starting at positions 0 and len. If `signature.length > signLength`, the extra trailing bytes are silently ignored. If `signature.length < signLength`, an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException would occur. The method does not validate that `signature.length == signLength` before processing, which could allow malformed signatures with trailing bytes to be processed without error, potentially accepting non-canonical JWS ECDSA signatures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ECDSA tests use platform-default EC keys for ES384 and ES512, so they do not test the required 48- and 66-byte coordinate curves or verify those algorithms work with their required curves.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that ECDSAAlgorithmTest uses KeyPairGenerator.getInstance('EC').genKeyPair() without specifying curve parameters, which will use the platform default curve (typically P-256). The test then runs the same keyPair against ES256, ES384, and ES512 algorithms. While the test verifies the ASN1 encoding/decoding roundtrip works, it doesn't actually test that the signature lengths match the expected curves (P-384 for ES384, P-521 for ES512). This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added crypto code.
